digest.definition: Accounting is studied as a social, economic and governance practice, a main form of information and control in every kind of organisation, not only as the measurement of profit and capital
distinctiveFeatures: Accounting is studied as a social, economic and governance practice, a main form of information and control in every kind of organisation, not only as the measurement of profit and capital
It joins the conceptual (theory and its social, sustainability, political and economic context) and the applied and technical; both are a floor
Judgement under uncertainty, ethics, professional scepticism and integrity in weighing evidence are at its core
It sits in a contested space between academic study and the accountancy bodies' professional requirements; the statement, not accreditation, sets the degree
Data and the systems that produce it are central, from double entry to ERP, analytics and AI
It looks forward: critical of current accounting, imagining other futures, sustainability accounting foremost, and preparing for rules that change within a career
Master's study comes in four taught types (advanced or specialist, conversion, professional, integrated), each with self-directed research-based inquiry; research master's are outside the statement

transferable.text: You are expected to present numbers, analysis and arguments clearly to different audiences, in speech, writing, visuals and other media.
You are expected to work well with others: listening, negotiating, persuading and leading, inclusively and with emotional intelligence, in teams and with other organisations.
You are expected to believe in and act on your own ability, reflect on your progress, take charge of your own learning and of the results of your actions, and bounce back from setbacks.
You are expected to weigh evidence, arguments and research critically, make judgements when things are uncertain, apply professional scepticism and take an ethical stand.
You are expected to work out the likely causes of a problem from the data, compare possible actions, including their ethics, and choose solutions that are ethical and sustainable.
You are expected to find, check and interpret data from different sources, draw reasoned conclusions even when the data is incomplete, and present what you find in a form your audience can use.
You are expected to see how processes connect as systems and to help analyse, design and improve the systems that produce data, including controls against error, fraud and cyber attack.
You are expected to handle and share data in all its forms, keep it secure and use and judge tools such as spreadsheets, databases and AI as new ones appear.
You are expected to use number skills to work with data and to evaluate, estimate and model business problems.
You are expected to show commercial awareness and business sense, with creativity, flexibility and new ideas, while keeping the public interest in mind.
You are expected to appreciate cultural differences and how they can shape accounting, study and organisations; if your course includes time abroad, another language helps too.
You are expected to carry out a careful, systematic investigation of your own: read critically, find credible sources, ask good questions, analyse, manage the project and present clear findings.

statements.about: the purpose of an Accounting degree
statements.paraphrase: An Accounting degree should prepare students to understand accounting in its social and economic setting and its part in responsible governance, audit and assurance, as a base for many careers and for ethical citizenship; it should look past profit and capital to accountability for sustainability and welfare, to the many kinds of organisation and stakeholder that use accounting, and to past and current research.

forPractitioner.text: Shape the course so that students see accounting as a social and economic practice tied to governance and accountability, across public, charitable, co-operative and private bodies and their stakeholders, not only as the measurement of profit and capital; ground it in foundational and current research.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you see what accounting does in society and in how organisations are governed, well beyond profit, including its part in sustainability and welfare and in the work of charities, public bodies and campaigns.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.about: designing for students with different aims
statements.paraphrase: Accounting degrees should be built to serve students who come to them for different reasons: a professional qualification, a route into business, government or other sectors, a wider social interest or the intellectual pursuit itself.

forPractitioner.text: Design for a mixed cohort: some students want a professional accountancy route, others business, public-sector or third-sector careers, social understanding or the subject for its own sake; the breadth of perspectives serves them all.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.about: accounting systems and the social sciences
statements.paraphrase: Students study how accounting systems shape and are shaped by theory, people, organisations, technology, markets, society and the environment; that study should draw on social science perspectives, for example politics, sociology, psychology, economics and information systems, with finance covered as the course's nature requires.

forPractitioner.text: Bring social science perspectives (economics, information systems, politics, psychology, sociology and others) into the study of how accounting systems are designed, run and validated, and size the finance content to the course type.

forBeneficiary.text: You will study how accounting systems affect, and are affected by, people, organisations, technology, markets, society and the environment, and your course should draw on ideas from economics, politics, sociology and other social sciences to help you.

statements.about: technical, non-critical content at the expense of breadth
statements.paraphrase: Pressures from employers, professional bodies, regulators and others can push courses towards technical, uncritical accounting; a degree that does so at the cost of the broader intellectual, social and environmental needs the statement sets out falls short of it.

forPractitioner.text: Check the design against accreditation pull: a course that trades the broader intellectual, social and environmental content for narrow technical material does not satisfy this statement, whatever exemptions it earns.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: An Accounting degree should ready students for a future in which standards and practice may change radically within a career, so a mainly technical degree is not enough; alongside current regulation and standards it should build lifelong, self-directed learning and professional, transferable and critical skills.

forPractitioner.text: Do not build the course around today's technical rules alone: they will change within your graduates' careers. Teach current frameworks, and build self-directed learning and professional, transferable and critical skills that keep graduates employable long term.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should prepare you for a profession whose rules and practices may change a great deal during your career, so it should help you keep learning on your own and build professional, transferable and critical skills, not only today's techniques.

statements.about: systems that provide data and information
statements.paraphrase: An Accounting degree should prepare students to understand how systems that provide data and information are designed and run: traditional double-entry bookkeeping and the preparation of statements, wider business systems for non-financial and further financial data (for sustainability, social reporting and compliance), and the analysis and evaluation of structured and unstructured data and the structures that hold it.

forPractitioner.text: Cover both the traditional accounting process (double entry, statement preparation) and wider business and data systems, including databases and ERP, so that students can question, analyse and evaluate structured and unstructured data for sustainability, social and compliance reporting.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you understand how accounting and wider business systems produce data and information, from double-entry bookkeeping to databases and ERP systems, and help you question, analyse and judge both tidy and messy data.

statements.about: critique of the status quo and other futures for accounting
statements.paraphrase: Courses need to give students the knowledge, skills and confidence to criticise current accounting, to propose other ways of accounting and organising business in the public interest, and to imagine futures for accounting, sustainability accounting among them; they should not be confined to accounting as it now stands.

forPractitioner.text: Plan for critique and imagination: students should question mainstream accounting, consider alternatives in the public interest and the common good, and envisage different futures, with sustainability accounting a central case.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should give you the confidence to question accounting as it is done today, to suggest other ways of doing it for the public good and to imagine how it could change, for example in accounting for sustainability.

statements.about: conceptual and applied study as a minimum
statements.paraphrase: Accounting is studied in both its conceptual and its applied aspects, conceptual covering accounting theory and broad social, sustainability, political and economic questions; a degree lacking substantial conceptual study does not reach the minimum, and nor does one that wholly leaves out the applied and technical side.

forPractitioner.text: Both halves are a floor, not an option: substantial conceptual study (theory and its social, sustainability, political and economic context) and real applied and technical study. A course missing either does not reach the minimum this statement sets.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.about: degree apprenticeships judged the same way
statements.paraphrase: Apprenticeship degrees should be measured against the same criteria as other Accounting degrees.

forPractitioner.text: Hold an Accounting degree apprenticeship to the same expectations as the full-time degree: the work-based route does not lower or narrow them.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.about: the advanced or specialist academic master's
statements.paraphrase: Advanced or specialist master's degrees study one or more main parts of an honours Accounting degree at an advanced theoretical level, sometimes with specialist subjects; their graduates are expected to reach honours-level attainment in those areas, meet extra content needs of the specialism and show independent, self-directed inquiry; entry normally needs a good honours degree mainly or jointly in Accounting.

forPractitioner.text: For an advanced or specialist master's, expect honours-level attainment in the areas studied, the extra content the specialism needs and independent, self-directed inquiry; plan for entrants with a good Accounting honours degree.

forBeneficiary.text: On an advanced or specialist master's in Accounting you are expected to reach at least honours-level attainment in your areas, master the extra content of your specialism and carry out independent inquiry of your own.

statements.paraphrase: Conversion master's degrees let students from other disciplines, or who met accounting in another jurisdiction, gain the essentials of an Accounting honours degree and go further at master's level; they should normally be guided by the standards for a good honours degree, with added master's expectations and independent inquiry; entry normally needs a good honours degree in another subject or equivalent experience.

forPractitioner.text: Design a conversion master's from the good-honours expectations upward: secure the core knowledge, understanding and skills of an Accounting honours degree, then extend some topics to master's level and require independent, self-directed inquiry.

forBeneficiary.text: On a conversion master's you should gain the core of what an Accounting honours graduate knows and can do, then take some topics further and complete an independent inquiry of your own.

statements.paraphrase: Professional master's degrees give professional-level knowledge, skills and critical thinking, with ethical judgement and scepticism in applied settings, for students seeking accreditation and exemptions; they will involve advanced study of main parts of an honours degree focused on high-level application, and their graduates are expected to reach and then extend honours-level attainment and show independent inquiry.

forPractitioner.text: A professional master's will study main areas of the honours degree at an advanced level with a strong focus on application, judgement and scepticism; expect graduates to go beyond honours attainment in professional content and to complete independent, self-directed inquiry.

forBeneficiary.text: On a professional master's you will study key areas of accounting at an advanced level with a strong focus on applying them, and you are expected to go beyond honours level and carry out an independent inquiry of your own.

statements.about: self-directed research-based study at master's level
statements.paraphrase: Every master's in Accounting should include a substantial piece of self-directed, research-based study, a personal inquiry into theory or into applying theory to a real project or issue, inside organisations or beyond them.

forPractitioner.text: Build a substantial self-directed, research-based component into every master's: a personal inquiry into a theoretical question or the application of theory to a real organisational, environmental, work or social issue.

forBeneficiary.text: Your master's should include a substantial inquiry that you direct yourself, into a theoretical question or into using theory on a real issue inside or outside an organisation.

statements.paraphrase: Integrated master's degrees usually add a year to the honours degree and are expected to reach the standards for a good honours degree and then those of an advanced or specialist master's, or in some jurisdictions a professional master's, including substantial self-directed research-based inquiry.

forPractitioner.text: Plan the integrated master's as good-honours attainment plus a further year that reaches the advanced or specialist (or professional) master's expectations, with a substantial self-directed inquiry.

forBeneficiary.text: On an integrated master's you are expected to reach a good honours standard and then go on to master's-level work in the final year, including a substantial inquiry of your own.
