statements.about: EDI built into the discipline and every course
statements.paraphrase: EDI spans many identity characteristics and forms of difference, beyond legal equality duties and including intersections across students and staff; it should be built meaningfully into the culture and practice of accounting and into every Accounting degree.

forPractitioner.text: Embed equality, diversity and inclusion in the culture of the department and in every course, attending to intersecting identities among students and staff, not only to legal duties.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.about: principles for an inclusive learning community
statements.paraphrase: To create an inclusive learning community, providers should draw on established principles and guidance for embedding EDI in the curriculum (enabling potential, belonging, awareness, appreciation of other views, self-reflection), with a conscious, proactive approach in environment, content and teaching.

forPractitioner.text: Use published principles for embedding EDI (enabling potential, belonging, awareness, respect for other perspectives, self-reflection) and act on them deliberately in the learning environment, content and teaching strategy.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.about: EDI in the curriculum and in reporting
statements.paraphrase: Through EDI, accounting education can help organisations tackle inequality (the SDGs on gender equality, decent work, reduced inequalities and strong institutions); the curriculum should build in EDI and continued reflection so students can thrive in a diverse world and act inclusively at work, and should give them an understanding of how reporting and record keeping can address these issues and the means and will to apply EDI in practice.

forPractitioner.text: Design EDI into the curriculum with reflective practice, and teach how reporting and record keeping can help address inequality, so that students leave with both the understanding and the tools to act inclusively at work.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you understand how reporting and record keeping can help tackle inequality, and give you the reflective habits and tools to work inclusively in your career.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.about: diverse content and critique of dominant approaches
statements.paraphrase: Courses should equip students to build diverse, inclusive workplaces and to see accounting's role in global challenges such as poverty, injustice and inequality; content should be diverse and should examine dominant approaches critically, drawing on perspectives from the Global South, marginalised and local communities, with examples that reflect the cohort and society.

forPractitioner.text: Diversify the content: examine dominant approaches critically, show how they can exclude, bring in voices from the Global South and marginalised and local communities, and use cases that reflect your students and wider society.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you see accounting's part in global problems such as poverty and inequality, question the usual ways of doing it and learn from a wide range of voices and places.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Courses should be designed so that students of every background can reach their potential and feel represented and included whatever their characteristics; learning, teaching and assessment should be inclusive, using varied modes and a broad range of assessment types, with alternatives where needed.

forPractitioner.text: Design every part, from mode of study to assessment type, so that students of all backgrounds can succeed and feel represented; offer alternative assessments where they remove disadvantage.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: EDI in a course needs continuous monitoring and review, and programme teams should regularly consider how well EDI policies are working and how to improve them, with students as partners where they can.

forPractitioner.text: Review EDI in the course regularly, ask how well policies have been put into practice and how to improve them, and involve students in that review.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree
Accessibility and the needs of disabled students

statements.paraphrase: Courses should commit to widening access and inclusive participation so every student can thrive whatever their background, disability or health; providers should anticipate needs and take responsibility for inclusive learning, teaching and assessment, and with support services will make reasonable adjustments proactively.

forPractitioner.text: Anticipate disabled students' needs rather than waiting for requests: take responsibility for inclusive learning, teaching and assessment and work with support services to make reasonable adjustments in advance.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree
Accessibility and the needs of disabled students

statements.about: meeting accessibility requirements at every stage
statements.paraphrase: On accessibility, providers should at the least meet the regulatory requirements, which run from pre-application information to graduation and after; the paragraph then lists practices that may help.

forPractitioner.text: Treat the legal accessibility requirements as the minimum across the whole student journey, from information before application to graduation and beyond.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree
Accessibility and the needs of disabled students

statements.about: proactive inclusive design and attainment gaps
statements.paraphrase: Learning, teaching and assessment should be designed proactively, including looking into possible attainment gaps, so that inclusivity and flexibility are built in for diverse needs.

forPractitioner.text: Investigate attainment gaps and use what you find to build inclusivity and flexibility into teaching and assessment from the start.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree
Accessibility and the needs of disabled students

statements.about: equal access to placements, study abroad and activities
statements.paraphrase: Where relevant, accessibility should aim to give all students the same or similar chances of workplace and international learning and of extra-curricular and co-curricular activity.

forPractitioner.text: Check that placements, study abroad and extra- and co-curricular activities are open on equal terms to disabled students and others with protected characteristics.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Courses should address sustainability in line with current thinking such as the United Nations', taking sustainable development in its widest sense of welfare and social, environmental and political perspectives, which is wider than ESG disclosure.

forPractitioner.text: Treat sustainability broadly, as welfare and social, environmental and political concerns in line with current UN thinking, not only as ESG disclosure.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: A degree should give students the capacity to use traditional and emerging accounting practices to support the move to a more sustainable and fairer world, as framed by the SDGs and PRME; to that end it should develop their technical, critical and transferable skills, higher-order thinking, ethics and forward-looking mindsets for steering organisations towards sustainable outcomes.

forPractitioner.text: Develop students' ability to apply established and emerging accounting practices to a sustainable, fairer transition, with the technical, critical, transferable, ethical and anticipatory capacities to steer organisations towards sustainable outcomes.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you use both established and new accounting practices to support a fairer and more sustainable world, and build the skills, ethics and forward thinking to help organisations get there.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.about: accounting as a catalyst for sustainable change
statements.paraphrase: Courses should show accounting and accountants as leaders of change: making sustainability visible, deciding how organisations' impacts are counted and reported, building in double materiality, valuing assets, increasing transparency and engaging diverse stakeholders.

forPractitioner.text: Show students accounting as a driver of change, through cases on making sustainability visible, double materiality, valuation, transparency and stakeholder engagement.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should show you how accountants can lead change, for example by making sustainability issues visible, deciding how impacts are counted and reported, and making organisations more transparent.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.about: accounting theories and practices for sustainable development
statements.paraphrase: Graduates should know and understand theories and practices of accounting, assurance and accountability that can help achieve sustainable development, and be able to evaluate critically how these or other approaches can lead to more sustainable results.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates should know the accounting, assurance and accountability theories and practices relevant to sustainable development and be able to judge critically which approaches produce more sustainable outcomes.

forBeneficiary.text: You should know the accounting, assurance and accountability ideas and practices that can support sustainable development, and be able to judge critically which ones work better.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Graduates should be capable of driving and leading the sustainability agenda for business and society, above all on the ethics, responsibility and sustainability expectations of accounting accrediting bodies and on EDI, and in growing sustainable entrepreneurial mindsets.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates should be able to take a lead on sustainability in organisations and society, meeting accrediting bodies' ethics and sustainability expectations and EDI responsibilities, with an entrepreneurial outlook.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to take the lead on sustainability in organisations and society, acting on the ethical and sustainability expectations of the profession and on equality and inclusion.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.about: accounting as a performative social practice
statements.paraphrase: Courses should be designed to prepare students to help organisations and society move to a more sustainable future, and should treat accounting and accountants as part of changing social, economic, organisational and political practices that bring about real change by making the consequences of decisions transparent.

forPractitioner.text: Prepare students to support organisations' sustainability transitions, and teach accounting as a practice that changes what happens by making the consequences of decisions visible.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should prepare you to help organisations move towards a sustainable future and show you how accounting changes what happens by making the results of decisions visible.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Courses should reflect current and emerging sustainability priorities that are reshaping accounting and assurance, such as net zero, regenerative business models, modern slavery, carbon and greenhouse gas management, plastics and waste, water, sustainable supply chains and new reporting and assurance standards.

forPractitioner.text: Keep the content current with sustainability priorities that are changing practice: net zero, carbon and greenhouse gas management, modern slavery, waste and water, supply chains and new sustainability reporting and assurance standards.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: A degree should prepare students to understand how information systems can embed sustainability throughout accounting and organisational systems and develop their skill in designing, analysing, transforming and managing sustainability data, including how it sits in data structures and ERP systems and how unstructured data can serve sustainability ends.

forPractitioner.text: Teach how sustainability data is built into accounting and organisational systems, including ERP and other data structures, and give students practice in designing, analysing, transforming and managing that data, structured and unstructured.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you understand how sustainability data is captured in accounting and business systems and build your skill in designing, analysing and managing that data.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Courses should stress critical enquiry into planetary boundaries and what sustainability means for growth, well-being and political stability, with students building critical thinking, self-awareness, confidence to raise issues, collaboration, anticipatory and systemic thinking and sound measurement, valuation and communication as a base for further study and lifelong learning.

forPractitioner.text: Make critical enquiry into planetary limits central, and through it develop critical, systemic, strategic and anticipatory thinking, self-awareness, collaboration, the confidence to raise issues and skill in measuring, valuing and communicating.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should push you to question how sustainability limits affect growth, well-being and politics, and help you think critically and systemically, work with others and speak up about issues.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Courses should weave economic, social and environmental sustainability through the whole curriculum, adding specialist modules on topics such as climate change or biodiversity where suitable.

forPractitioner.text: Integrate sustainability across all modules first; add specialist modules (on climate or biodiversity, for example) as a complement, not a substitute.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Enterprise education develops the capacity to generate ideas and the behaviours to realise them, and entrepreneurship applies them to create cultural, social or economic value; including both improves employability, and courses should include them to produce enterprising, flexible and innovative graduates who can handle a changing workplace with confidence and creativity.

forPractitioner.text: Include enterprise and entrepreneurship so that students learn to generate ideas and act on them, and leave enterprising, adaptable and innovative enough to handle a changing workplace.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you come up with ideas and make them happen, so that you can work with confidence, flexibility and creativity in a fast-changing workplace.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.about: critical thinkers who can act on ideas
statements.paraphrase: Courses should make students critical thinkers who can generate and carry out new ideas, to be entrepreneurial (self-employment included) and employable in any sector; enterprise education should add to their cultural, social and economic values and fit them for lifelong learning, a self-directed career and many career paths.

forPractitioner.text: Develop critical thinking as the base for generating and carrying out ideas, whether in self-employment or in any sector, and link enterprise education to students' values and lifelong learning.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you think critically and turn ideas into action, whether you work for yourself or for others, and prepare you to keep learning across many possible careers.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.about: enterprise skills through the core content
statements.paraphrase: Covering the core principles of the subject should develop enterprise-related skills and attributes, and research-led and research-informed teaching should be used to grow open-mindedness, proactivity, determination, resilience and self-efficacy; enterprise skills should also come through seeing that knowing alternative accounting options supports negotiation, creative problem-solving, judgement, leadership, commercial awareness and business acumen.

forPractitioner.text: Use research-led teaching and the subject's core principles to build open-mindedness, proactivity, resilience and self-efficacy, and show how knowing alternative accounting treatments strengthens negotiation, problem-solving, judgement and commercial sense.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you become open-minded, proactive and resilient, and show you how knowing different accounting options helps you negotiate, solve problems and make sound business judgements.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Courses should cover how GenAI is used in accounting practice, build students' skill with suitable professional GenAI tools and develop critical thinking about the limits and implications of those tools; since AI is already common in practice software, analytics and audit planning, degrees need to keep adapting.

forPractitioner.text: Teach where GenAI is used in accounting work, give students hands-on practice with suitable professional tools, and develop their critical view of the tools' limits; review the content often as practice changes.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should show you how GenAI is used in accounting work, give you practice with suitable tools and help you think critically about what those tools cannot do.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Because AI learns from existing text and decisions it can spread bias (by gender, race, class or capitalist logic) unless controlled, and the control can itself be biased; providers need to know this, and courses should develop students' understanding of bias and discrimination in AI and how to reduce them.

forPractitioner.text: Teach how AI systems can reproduce bias and discrimination, and how that can be reduced; be alert to the same risk in the tools the course itself uses.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you understand how AI systems can repeat bias and discrimination and what can be done to reduce it.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Courses should use GenAI to support learning, for example to make teaching more interactive, to provide AI-written answers for students to critique and compare with their own writing, and to support dialogic and experiential learning; students should learn to use technology with integrity, linked to the profession's ethics.

forPractitioner.text: Use GenAI for learning on purpose: interactive teaching, critiquing AI-written answers, comparison with students' own work for inner feedback; teach integrity in its use and connect it to professional ethics.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should use GenAI to help you learn, for example by asking you to critique AI-written answers and compare them with your own, and help you use such tools honestly and ethically.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.about: assessment design in the age of GenAI
statements.paraphrase: GenAI makes it essential to rethink assessment: it can move assessment away from rote and multiple-choice formats towards critical, authentic, case-based and experiential tasks, including assessment of students' grasp of AI in accounting; these points should be weighed in formative and summative assessment alike.

forPractitioner.text: Redesign assessment for GenAI: move away from rote and objective formats towards authentic cases, dynamic scenarios and experiential tasks, assess understanding of AI in accounting, and apply this to formative and summative work.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Providers are responsible for due diligence to keep assessment rigorous and honest despite GenAI: clear, consistently applied integrity and GenAI-aware quality policies, awareness of misuse by students and staff, continuous review, since detection is unreliable, and policies communicated to everyone involved.

forPractitioner.text: Put GenAI-aware integrity policies in place, apply them consistently, review them continuously because detection is unreliable, and make sure students and staff know them.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.about: design aims of an Accounting degree
statements.paraphrase: Courses should be designed so students can build a broad, rigorous understanding of accounting in its social and economic setting, make sound and creative judgements on complex problems, understand accounting across kinds of organisation and stakeholder and in issues such as sustainability, EDI and accessibility, and become responsible, ethical citizens.

forPractitioner.text: Design for breadth and rigour: accounting in context, sound and creative judgement on complex problems, many kinds of organisation and stakeholder, sustainability, EDI and accessibility, and ethical citizenship.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should be designed to give you a broad, rigorous understanding of accounting in society, the ability to make sound judgements on complex problems and the grounding to act as a responsible, ethical citizen.

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.about: learning objectives aligned to the statement
statements.paraphrase: Courses should set learning objectives in line with section 3's knowledge, understanding and skills and with sound learning, teaching and assessment principles; institutional structures should shape but not overly limit the design; objectives should join the conceptual and applied and link areas of knowledge, with room to adapt to change in the subject and to technology such as GenAI.

forPractitioner.text: Write programme objectives that map to the knowledge, understanding and skills in section 3, join conceptual and applied study and connect areas, and keep the design flexible enough to adapt to new technology.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Courses should be designed so students develop the higher-order intellectual skills needed in a changing, increasingly automated society and workplace, and a degree should prepare them for lifelong, self-directed learning.

forPractitioner.text: Give priority to higher-order thinking (analysis, evaluation, creativity) over routine tasks that automation will absorb, and build habits of self-directed, lifelong learning.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should develop your higher-level thinking, such as analysis, evaluation and creativity, for a workplace where routine tasks are increasingly automated, and prepare you to keep learning on your own.

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Courses should be designed so students can succeed in a range of careers, entrepreneurial ventures or academic paths.

forPractitioner.text: Keep career routes open: design for employment in many sectors, for entrepreneurship and for academic study, not only for professional accountancy.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should prepare you to do well in many kinds of career, in starting something of your own or in further academic study.

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.about: accreditation not at the expense of breadth
statements.paraphrase: Many students hope to qualify professionally, but courses should take account of students' wider and changing aims and should not be designed to win PSRB exemptions and accreditation at the cost of the broader aims of section 3.

forPractitioner.text: Seek accreditation where it helps students, but do not let exemption requirements drive out the broader design aims; plan for students whose career aims change.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Joint degrees with Accounting should be designed to include most of the statement's knowledge, understanding and skills, with a balance that still keeps conceptual issues, theory, accountability, sustainability, non-business uses, application and higher-order thinking.

forPractitioner.text: In a joint degree, cover most of the statement's knowledge and skills and keep the balance from squeezing out conceptual, accountability, sustainability and higher-order content.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.appliesTo: combined or joint honours with Accounting
statements.paraphrase: In combined or joint honours, progression requirements will be designed to meet the progression needs of both subjects.

forPractitioner.text: Set progression rules for a joint or combined honours route that satisfy both subjects' needs, not only the larger one.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.about: progression that allows for individual needs
statements.paraphrase: Progression should allow for each student's needs and, where it is relevant and feasible, permit reasonable adjustments, so that every student can reach their potential.

forPractitioner.text: Build flexibility for individual needs into progression rules, including reasonable adjustments where possible.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.about: honours as a basis for qualification and careers
statements.paraphrase: An honours degree in Accounting should give a sound base for a professional qualification or other careers, especially in business or finance.

forPractitioner.text: Make sure the honours degree gives a sound foundation for professional qualification and for other careers, notably in business and finance.

forBeneficiary.text: Your honours degree should give you a sound start towards a professional qualification or another career, especially in business or finance.

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates with a second-class degree or higher
statements.paraphrase: A student with at least a second-class degree should be ready for postgraduate study in Accounting or a related subject, though entry is for each provider to set; the same principles normally govern progression to the master's year of an integrated master's.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates with a second-class degree or better should be ready for postgraduate study in the subject; admissions decisions remain each institution's, and the same principles apply to entering an integrated master's final year.

forBeneficiary.text: If you gain a second-class degree or higher, you should be ready for postgraduate study in Accounting or a related subject, though each institution sets its own entry rules.

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Similar progression standards will apply to degree apprentices at honours level (FHEQ 6, FQHEIS 10), and apprentices may also need to pass an end-point assessment.

forPractitioner.text: Apply the same progression standards to degree apprentices as to other students, and plan for the end-point assessment the apprenticeship may require.

forBeneficiary.text: As a degree apprentice, the same progression standards will apply to you, and you may also need to pass an end-point assessment to complete the apprenticeship.

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Courses need to adapt to, and anticipate, advances in the subject and related fields and the needs of graduates and employers, and should be flexible enough to serve learners, the profession, wider stakeholders and external bodies' requirements.

forPractitioner.text: Review and adapt the course as the subject and employers' needs change, and keep it flexible enough to meet learners', the profession's and external bodies' needs.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.about: inclusive flexibility of mode and length
statements.paraphrase: Courses should be planned with inclusion in mind and may vary learning mode and assessment to suit students; flexibility can come from length (a placement or study abroad year), mode (full or part-time, in person or distance), entry criteria and assessment.

forPractitioner.text: Design for inclusivity through options in length, mode, entry criteria and assessment, such as placement years, part-time and distance study.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Degree-awarding bodies may deliver with partners; the statement should be applied so the standards are met across the whole partnership course, and courses designed with partners should not be built for PSRB exemption and accreditation at the cost of the broader aims.

forPractitioner.text: Apply the statement across the whole of a partnership course so that the standards hold everywhere, and do not let a partner's accreditation aims narrow the design.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: PSRBs, above all the professional accountancy bodies, can be important partners in design and courses may reflect their recognition requirements, but every Accounting degree should meet this statement's standards rather than have its content set by PSRB accreditation.

forPractitioner.text: Work with professional bodies, but measure the course against this statement's standards first; accreditation requirements do not replace them.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Monitoring and regular review are central to quality; degree-awarding bodies should use a range of external reference points, relevant subject statements among them, to keep provision in line with sector norms, through annual and periodic review with external input.

forPractitioner.text: Use external reference points, this statement included, in annual monitoring and periodic review, with external experts or advisers, to keep the course in line with the sector.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Monitoring and evaluation should check that sustainable development, EDI, accessibility, enterprise and entrepreneurship and GenAI run through the curriculum and show in learning, teaching and assessment design.

forPractitioner.text: Use monitoring and review to check that the five themes are present across the curriculum and in teaching and assessment, not in one module only.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: External examiners help keep standards consistent across the sector by commenting on assessment, marking, modules and outcomes, and reporting yearly; this statement and others, especially their standards, should have a central place in their evaluation and advice.

forPractitioner.text: Ask external examiners to judge the course and its outcomes against this statement's standards, and use their reports in review.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Accounting degree

statements.paraphrase: Courses aligned with PSRBs face extra monitoring by those bodies for exemption and accreditation, through visits and desk reviews; providers should tell prospective and current students about their routes to a professional qualification.

forPractitioner.text: Give prospective and current students clear information about how the course leads to professional qualification and which exemptions it carries.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.about: content shaped by section 1 and the themes
statements.paraphrase: Course content should follow section 1's principles, be shaped mainly by the purposes and characteristics subsection and reflect the cross-cutting themes.

forPractitioner.text: Derive the content from section 1's purposes and characteristics and carry the cross-cutting themes into it.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.about: the public interest role of accounting
statements.paraphrase: Courses should give real weight to accounting's public interest role and accountability, society's present and future needs and critique of current accounting, encouraging students to imagine other futures; degrees need to instil responsibility and readiness for change, grounded in ethics.

forPractitioner.text: Give substantial time to the public interest and accountability, to critique of current accounting and to imagining alternatives, and build an ethical sense of responsibility and anticipation of change.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should give real weight to accounting's role in the public interest, encourage you to question how it is done now and help you imagine other ways, with a sense of ethical responsibility.

statements.paraphrase: Courses should encourage critical discussion of accounting and accountability in their social and economic setting, rest on social science perspectives, and look past profit and capital to accountability for sustainability, welfare and social, environmental and political concerns.

forPractitioner.text: Teach accounting critically and in context, drawing on the social sciences and treating accountability for sustainability, welfare and social concerns as core.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should get you discussing accounting critically in its social and economic setting and looking beyond profit to sustainability, welfare and social concerns.

statements.about: accounting across many kinds of organisation
statements.paraphrase: Courses rest on accounting as a main form of information and control in many organisations (public, charitable, co-operative, social enterprise, campaigning and for-profit) and should include applying accounting knowledge, skills and critique to a range of them.

forPractitioner.text: Give students practice in applying accounting knowledge, skills and critique to public, charitable, co-operative, social enterprise and campaigning bodies as well as companies.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should give you practice in using and questioning accounting in many kinds of organisation, from charities and public bodies to co-operatives and companies.

statements.paraphrase: Courses should cover both the conceptual and theoretical and the applied sides of accounting.

forPractitioner.text: Include both conceptual and theoretical study and applied study in every course.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.about: accounting beyond numbers in a complex world
statements.paraphrase: Courses should not be only about numbers or money, since accounting deals with accountability and much non-financial information; they should prepare students to learn from accounting's history and to apply their knowledge and skills to guide organisations through modern complexity, including sustainability, stakeholder expectations, social and welfare issues and questions with no settled answer.

forPractitioner.text: Go beyond financial numbers: teach accounting's history, its non-financial reporting and its role in sustainability, stakeholder expectations and social issues, and give students practice in guiding organisations through ambiguous problems.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should show you that accounting is about more than numbers and money, and prepare you to use what you learn to guide organisations through complex social, sustainability and ethical questions.

statements.paraphrase: Courses should build in subject-specific skills so students understand accounting knowledge and can apply it in practice, including recording and summarising transactions, preparing financial statements, analysing operations (decisions, performance, control, budgets, discounted cash flow) and financial analysis and projection.

forPractitioner.text: Make sure students practise recording and summarising transactions, preparing financial statements, analysing operations (decision analysis, performance measurement, budgeting, discounted cash flow) and analysing ratios, risks and projections.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should build your practical accounting skills: recording transactions, preparing financial statements, analysing how a business performs and projecting its finances.

statements.about: the broad areas of knowledge, integrated
statements.paraphrase: Courses should cover all of the broad areas listed, in varying combinations and with overlap; each area should include theory, current practice, regulation, current debate and application in complex settings with evidence-based judgement, in local, national and global contexts, developed to rising levels and taught as connected parts of accounting rather than separate silos, with their links to the themes recognised.

forPractitioner.text: Cover every listed area, each with theory, practice, regulation, debate and application in local, national and global contexts; teach them as linked parts of accounting, build them up across the years, and show how the themes cut across them.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.about: area a: accountability, responsibility and trust
statements.paraphrase: Area a: accounting helps organisations create sustainable value ethically, and accountants carry a duty to communicate openly and reliably to many stakeholders; a course should equip students to see this position of trust, judge well and give assurance, advice and leadership.

forPractitioner.text: Teach the position of trust accountants hold and give students practice in judgement, assurance, advice and leadership that honours it.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you see the trust placed in accountants and build your ability to judge well and to give assurance, advice and leadership.

statements.about: area b: the business, social and economic environment
statements.paraphrase: Area b: a course should look at the business, social and economic setting, and graduates should show they know how that environment affects organisations, and organisations it, locally to internationally, across environmental, cultural, ethical, legal, tax, political, social and technological factors.

forPractitioner.text: Cover the environment organisations work in and their effect on it, at local, national and international scale, across environmental, cultural, ethical, legal, tax, political, social and digital factors.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to show that you understand how the business, economic and social environment shapes organisations, and how organisations shape it in turn.

statements.paraphrase: Area c: ethics means spotting dilemmas, understanding their effects, judging and acting well, for organisations and society and for accounting in particular; both should be taught, woven through the degree so students can apply professional scepticism, handle complex moral situations and decide in the public interest.

forPractitioner.text: Weave ethics through the whole degree, general and accounting-specific, so students practise scepticism, work through hard moral cases and decide in the public interest.

forBeneficiary.text: Ethics should run through your whole course, helping you spot dilemmas, apply professional scepticism and make decisions that serve the public interest.

statements.about: area d: organisational governance and corporate reporting
statements.paraphrase: Area d: reporting covers preparing, analysing and interpreting all reports to stakeholders, financial and non-financial; a course should make sure graduates can apply the laws, regulations and standards with sound recording skills, know accounting's role in governance (groups included) and know current theory and research so they can judge practice critically.

forPractitioner.text: Teach the full range of reports, financial and non-financial, the laws and standards that govern them, recording skills, accounting's governance role and current research, so that graduates can evaluate practice critically.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to apply the laws, regulations and standards for reporting, understand accounting's part in how organisations are governed and use current research to judge reporting practice.

statements.paraphrase: Area e: providing timely, relevant financial and non-financial information for planning, performance, control and strategy, including decision methods, communication to decision-makers and strategic management accounting; a course should equip students to build and run performance measurement systems and KPIs, set and track budgets, apply costing and valuation, solve problems with incomplete or ambiguous data, anticipate risks and use technology and analytics.

forPractitioner.text: Give students practice in performance measurement systems and KPIs, budgeting, costing and valuation, communicating to decision-makers and solving problems with incomplete data, using analytics and current technology.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should prepare you to design and run performance measures, build and monitor budgets, apply costing and valuation, and make sound recommendations even when the data is incomplete.

statements.about: area f: systems, processes and data structures
statements.paraphrase: Area f: data and its processing are central, so courses need to cover how systems that supply data are designed, run and controlled, both traditional bookkeeping, ledgers and statements and wider systems for non-financial data, with graduates able to question, analyse and work with structured and unstructured data and the structures that hold it.

forPractitioner.text: Cover double entry, ledgers and statement production alongside wider data systems, databases and ERP, and give students practice with structured and unstructured data.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you understand how accounting and wider data systems work, from ledgers to databases, and build your skill in working with both tidy and messy data.

statements.paraphrase: Area g: the rules and norms governing accounting, the profession and accountable organisations in every sector, which let graduates see why financial system integrity and governance matter, covering governance codes, sustainability reporting rules, tax law and ethics, sustainability reporting and EDI.

forPractitioner.text: Teach the regulation of accounting, the profession and organisations in all sectors, including governance codes, sustainability reporting rules and tax law, and how ethics and equality enter regulation.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you understand the rules that govern accounting and organisations, from governance codes to sustainability reporting and tax law, and why they matter.

statements.paraphrase: Area h: courses should give students the knowledge to prepare for, and deliver, good audit and assurance that strengthens trust and transparency in financial and non-financial reporting, centred on scepticism, critical thinking, the public interest and professional judgement, and should firmly promote professional ethics so graduates can handle audit practice and standards confidently.

forPractitioner.text: Teach audit and assurance with professional scepticism, critical thinking and public interest responsibility at the centre, for financial and non-financial reporting, and stress professional ethics throughout.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should prepare you to carry out good audit and assurance work, with professional scepticism, sound judgement and a clear sense of the public interest.

statements.paraphrase: Area i: it is essential that courses equip students to handle the principles and complexity of tax and its social and economic purposes, the ethics and law of compliance and avoidance, and should promote transparency and the integrity of tax systems; at the least they should cover the main UK taxes, including income tax, National Insurance, capital gains, inheritance, corporation tax and VAT.

forPractitioner.text: Cover tax principles, purposes and ethics, the consequences of non-compliance and illicit practice, and at minimum the main UK taxes (income tax, National Insurance, capital gains, inheritance, corporation tax and VAT).

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you understand how tax works and why, the ethics and law around it and, at the least, the main UK taxes such as income tax, National Insurance, corporation tax and VAT.

statements.about: area j: uncertainty and risk management
statements.paraphrase: Area j: courses should prepare graduates for the complexity of organisational settings, with knowledge of risk and uncertainty and how they differ, of protecting assets and compliance, and of management and mitigation, so they can apply techniques such as risk appetite, scenario planning, game theory, decision trees and forecasting and advise on the data to use.

forPractitioner.text: Teach the difference between risk and uncertainty and give students practice with risk appetite, scenario planning, decision trees, forecasting and the data those models need.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you tell risk from uncertainty, use tools such as scenario planning, decision trees and forecasting, and advise on the right data for them.

statements.about: area k: data analytics and statistics
statements.paraphrase: Area k: analytics and statistics inform decisions and help in reading research; they allow large datasets to be interpreted, hypotheses tested and anomalies and trends found, with coding, search, AI and machine learning increasingly relevant; courses should include knowledge and applied skill in a range of these, with critical interpretation of results.

forPractitioner.text: Give students applied practice in analytics and statistics (hypothesis testing, anomaly detection and trend analysis, with some coding and machine learning), with critical reading of results and of research papers.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should give you practical skills in data analytics and statistics, and help you read the results, and the research that uses them, critically.

statements.about: area l: financial markets and institutions
statements.paraphrase: Area l: knowledge of financial markets and institutions is essential because accounting is central to how markets work; coverage depends on the degree, but at minimum a course is expected to include the time value of money, sources of finance, capital markets and instruments, project and corporate finance, stock exchanges, asset pricing, alternative, behavioural and personal finance and ethics in finance, with further topics optional.

forPractitioner.text: At minimum cover time value of money, sources of corporate finance, capital markets, project and corporate finance, asset pricing, behavioural and personal finance and ethics in finance; add further finance topics to suit the course.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course will cover the essentials of financial markets and institutions, such as the time value of money, sources of finance, capital markets, asset pricing and ethics in finance.

statements.paraphrase: The skills asked of a student completing the degree should follow the broad principles of section 1.

forPractitioner.text: Derive the skills the course develops from section 1's principles.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.about: skills that put knowledge into action
statements.paraphrase: Students should develop skills to show, apply and put into practice their knowledge and understanding, technical accounting skills included, to stay alert to context and the themes, and to act ethically.

forPractitioner.text: Students should build skills that turn their knowledge into practice, technical skills included, while staying aware of context and the themes and acting ethically.

forBeneficiary.text: You should develop the skills to show and use what you know in practice, including technical accounting skills, while keeping the wider context in view and acting ethically.

statements.paraphrase: Skill m: presenting quantitative and qualitative data, analysis and argument to suit different audiences and stakeholders, in spoken, written, visual and other forms and media.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to communicate data, analysis and argument effectively to different audiences, in speech, writing, visuals and varied media.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to present numbers, analysis and arguments clearly to different audiences, in speech, writing, visuals and other media.

statements.paraphrase: Skill n: listening, negotiating, persuading and communicating so as to work across boundaries, influence and collaborate inclusively and lead, including emotionally intelligent teamwork and work with other organisations and stakeholders.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to collaborate inclusively and with emotional intelligence in teams and across organisations, using listening, negotiation and persuasion, and to show leadership.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to work well with others: listening, negotiating, persuading and leading, inclusively and with emotional intelligence, in teams and with other organisations.

statements.about: skill o: self-efficacy and lifelong learning
statements.paraphrase: Skill o: belief in and ability to act on one's own capacity, with reflection and commitment to independent action, tied to self-managed lifelong learning: owning one's development and the results of one's actions, ethical decisions, resilience and prioritising.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to show self-efficacy: confidence in their own ability, reflection, independent action, ownership of their development, resilience and the ability to prioritise.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to believe in and act on your own ability, reflect on your progress, take charge of your own learning and of the results of your actions, and bounce back from setbacks.

statements.about: skill p: critical thinking and scepticism
statements.paraphrase: Skill p: critical and reflective evaluation of evidence, argument, theory and research, including judgement under uncertainty and ambiguity, scepticism as applied critical thinking, the nature of rationality, reflection and an ethical, activist stance.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to evaluate evidence, arguments, theory and research critically, judge under uncertainty, apply scepticism and take an ethical stance.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to weigh evidence, arguments and research critically, make judgements when things are uncertain, apply professional scepticism and take an ethical stand.

statements.about: skill q: problem solving and reasoning
statements.paraphrase: Skill q: analysing data and information in structured and messy situations to find a problem's likely causes, weighing alternative actions with ethical reasoning, and choosing ethical and sustainable solutions.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to diagnose problems from data in structured and unstructured situations, compare options with ethical reasoning and choose ethical, sustainable solutions.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to work out the likely causes of a problem from the data, compare possible actions, including their ethics, and choose solutions that are ethical and sustainable.

statements.paraphrase: Skill r: identifying, collecting and checking data from referenced sources in varied forms, then filtering, evaluating and interpreting it to reach reasoned conclusions, including for complex real problems with incomplete data and unclear aims, and presenting findings suitably, visualisations included.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to source, verify, filter, evaluate and interpret data, reach reasoned conclusions on messy real problems and present findings to suit the audience, using visualisation where it helps.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to find, check and interpret data from different sources, draw reasoned conclusions even when the data is incomplete, and present what you find in a form your audience can use.

statements.paraphrase: Skill s: seeing processes as interconnected systems and understanding the structures beneath complex situations, such as accounting and control systems, including analysing, designing, running, communicating, evaluating and improving systems that supply data, and managing risk, error, fraud and cyber threats, resilience, sustainability and assurance.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to think in systems: analyse, design, evaluate and improve the systems that supply data for reporting and decisions, including their controls against error, fraud and cyber risk.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to see how processes connect as systems and to help analyse, design and improve the systems that produce data, including controls against error, fraud and cyber attack.

statements.paraphrase: Skill t: using and evaluating sources and contexts of data, handling and communicating it in all forms, with attention to storage, control and cyber security, and using and assessing current technologies such as spreadsheets, databases and AI as they emerge.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to handle, communicate and secure data in all forms and to use and evaluate spreadsheets, databases, AI and new technologies as they arrive.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to handle and share data in all its forms, keep it secure and use and judge tools such as spreadsheets, databases and AI as new ones appear.

statements.paraphrase: Skill u: applying quantitative skills to work with data and to estimate, evaluate and model business problems, functions and phenomena.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to use quantitative skills to manipulate data and to evaluate, estimate and model business problems.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to use number skills to work with data and to evaluate, estimate and model business problems.

statements.paraphrase: Skill v: commercial awareness and business acumen, shown through innovation, creativity, flexibility, regard for the public interest and enterprise skills.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to show commercial awareness, business acumen, innovation, creativity and flexibility, with regard to the public interest and enterprise skills.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to show commercial awareness and business sense, with creativity, flexibility and new ideas, while keeping the public interest in mind.

statements.paraphrase: Skill w: appreciating cultural differences and their possible effects on the discipline, on study and on organisations; where a course includes work or study abroad, ability in another language matters too.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to appreciate cultural differences and how they affect the discipline, study and organisations; on courses with time abroad, foreign language ability also matters.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to appreciate cultural differences and how they can shape accounting, study and organisations; if your course includes time abroad, another language helps too.

statements.paraphrase: Skill x: combining earlier skills to carry out a systematic, robust investigation that reaches an informed conclusion on an issue: engaging critically with literature, finding credible sources, framing questions, analysing, managing the project and presenting findings clearly, to add knowledge or drive change.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates are expected to plan and complete a systematic investigation: critical use of literature, credible sources, focused questions, analysis, project management and clear reporting of findings.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to carry out a careful, systematic investigation of your own: read critically, find credible sources, ask good questions, analyse, manage the project and present clear findings.

statements.paraphrase: Learning and teaching strategies will be designed so students build conceptual and applied knowledge, higher-order thinking, technical accounting skills and relevant professional and transferable skills.

forPractitioner.text: Design the learning and teaching strategy to develop conceptual and applied knowledge, higher-order thinking, technical skills and professional and transferable skills together.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: Methods will be designed so activities align with intended outcomes, and teaching should be coherent with assessment, balance conceptual and applied study and encourage continuous learning and enquiry, giving students an appetite for lifelong learning.

forPractitioner.text: Align activities with intended outcomes and with assessment, balance conceptual and applied work and encourage continuing enquiry and lifelong learning.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: Learning and teaching should be designed to build skills, competencies, attitudes and experiences that help students become employable professionals and responsible citizens; some courses allow or require a placement for applying learning outside.

forPractitioner.text: Design teaching to build employability and civic responsibility together; where possible offer placements where students apply their learning.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you build the skills, attitudes and experience to become an employable professional and a responsible citizen, sometimes through a placement.

statements.paraphrase: Teaching may draw on critical, dialogic, reflexive, collaborative and constructivist approaches, alone or mixed; whatever is chosen should lead to deep learning, in which students think critically about new concepts, rather than rote learning, and should guide assessment choices and intellectual growth.

forPractitioner.text: Choose pedagogies (dialogic, critical, reflexive, constructivist, collaborative) that produce deep rather than rote learning, and let them shape assessment.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: A range of approaches should be encouraged within and across modules, from lectures, seminars, workshops and tutorials to blended, active and innovative learning; digital technologies matter because practice uses them, and approaches should be designed for engagement and active participation.

forPractitioner.text: Mix lectures, seminars, workshops, tutorials, blended and active learning, use the digital tools practice uses, and design for student engagement.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: Because a degree should prepare students to understand data systems, it will very probably be necessary to build suitable digital technology into teaching: cloud accounting packages, data cleaning and analytics tools, spreadsheets, AI including GenAI and emerging technology.

forPractitioner.text: Build current digital tools into teaching: cloud accounting packages, data preparation and analytics tools, spreadsheets and AI, refreshed as practice changes.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.about: inclusive, accessible and culturally aware teaching
statements.paraphrase: Learning and teaching should be inclusive and accessible by design and, ideally, should address the varied cultures and learning settings students come from, helping them move into a critical learning environment and learn from others about the global context.

forPractitioner.text: Design teaching to be inclusive and accessible, and help students from varied educational cultures adjust to critical learning and learn from one another.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should be inclusive and accessible, and help you adjust if you are used to a different way of learning, and learn from classmates with other backgrounds.

statements.paraphrase: Teaching, research and professional practice interact in the learning setting, and teaching should be research-informed or research-led; staff should be encouraged to draw on their professional and academic experience so teaching reflects current developments.

forPractitioner.text: Keep teaching research-informed or research-led, and draw on staff's professional and academic experience to reflect current developments.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: Teaching design can usefully draw on pedagogic research; strategies should adapt to business and regulatory change and technology, and teaching staff are expected to have access to professional development and suitable training.

forPractitioner.text: Update strategies for business, regulatory and technological change, use pedagogic research and give teaching staff professional development and training.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: The strategy, structures and approaches for teaching should be kept under continual review for quality and currency.

forPractitioner.text: Review the learning and teaching strategy continually, through the monitoring and review cycle, for quality and currency.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: Summative assessment should be robust and rigorous in measuring students' attainment of the statement's knowledge, understanding and skills as built into the course's learning outcomes.

forPractitioner.text: Make summative assessment robust and rigorous against the knowledge, understanding and skills in the statement as written into the outcomes.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: Alongside summative assessment, courses should include varied formative assessment and feedback, designed to enrich the learning setting and promote active, independent learning.

forPractitioner.text: Provide a range of formative assessments and feedback that encourage active, independent learning.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: The assessment portfolio across the degree should be balanced, with a fitting range of methods, so that it is inclusive, flexible and innovative, supports learning and lets students show rising attainment.

forPractitioner.text: Balance assessment methods across the degree so the scheme is inclusive, flexible and innovative and shows progression.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: Across the degree, assessment should make sure all required knowledge and skills are achieved, including the discursive, conceptual and critical, and should not let students avoid them by concentrating on routine, calculative and technical work.

forPractitioner.text: Weight and structure assessment so students cannot pass by focusing on calculation and technique alone; the discursive and critical elements must be unavoidable.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: Assessment should test depth of learning and skill, avoiding designs that let students pass through rote or surface learning such as objective tests; modules should include substantial critical assessment, authentic cases and technical questions set in dynamic scenarios, and any multiple choice should be designed not to reward uncritical learning.

forPractitioner.text: Design out rote learning: include substantial critical, authentic and case-based assessment, embed technical questions in dynamic scenarios and use multiple choice only where it is designed not to reward surface learning.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: The assessment strategy should be designed and run to make students independent, self-directed lifelong learners and critical thinkers, with feedback that helps their future learning.

forPractitioner.text: Design assessment and feedback to develop independent, self-directed and critical learners, with feedback aimed at the next task.

forBeneficiary.text: Your assessments and feedback should help you become an independent, critical learner who keeps learning after graduation.

statements.paraphrase: Assessment should be inclusive for EDI and accessibility, with reasonable adjustments where suitable that leave the assessment's nature, scope and outcomes intact; overall it should let students show what they have achieved.

forPractitioner.text: Make assessment inclusive and accessible, with reasonable adjustments that keep the assessment's purpose and the outcomes intact.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: Summative and formative assessment should support dialogues of learning that help students learn and become lifelong learners; feedback can take many forms, including students comparing their work with exemplars, peers' work, GenAI outputs or theory, and feedback schemes should be timely and usable.

forPractitioner.text: Design assessment as dialogue: use exemplars, peer work and GenAI outputs for students to compare against their own, and give timely feedback they can act on.

forBeneficiary.text: Your assessments should help you learn through dialogue, for example by comparing your work with examples, classmates' work or AI outputs, and you should get feedback in time to use it.

statements.paraphrase: Each module's assessment scheme should be clear to students at its start, and programme schemes should take account of timing and total workload.

forPractitioner.text: Publish each module's assessment scheme at the start and plan the timing and total assessment load across the programme.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: Assessment criteria should be communicated to students in good time, normally before they start work on the task; rubrics should normally be indicative and linked to learning outcomes rather than prescriptive.

forPractitioner.text: Give students the criteria before they begin each task, using indicative rubrics linked to module and programme outcomes rather than detailed marking schedules.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: Group assessment can suit collaborative skills; where it is used, grades should fairly reflect individuals' attainment, the balance with individual work should be weighed, and students should get guidance on running teams.

forPractitioner.text: Where you assess group work, make grades reflect individual contributions, balance it with individual work and teach students how to manage teams.

forBeneficiary.text: Where you are assessed as a group, your grade should fairly reflect your own contribution, and you should get guidance on how to run a team.

statements.paraphrase: Peer discussion and review can aid learning, but it should be well managed with safeguards so no one is disadvantaged, especially for EDI reasons; students should normally have guidance or training, and peer ratings should not normally count towards summative marks without strong protection and academic input.

forPractitioner.text: Manage peer review with safeguards and training; keep peer ratings out of summative marks unless strong protections and academic oversight are in place.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: Widespread GenAI means assessment design must account for AI, but it also allows designs closer to the statement's aims, such as critical, authentic, case-based and experiential tasks and assessment of students' grasp of AI in accounting; these points should apply to formative and summative work.

forPractitioner.text: Rework assessment for GenAI: authentic cases, dynamic scenarios, experiential tasks and assessment of students' understanding of AI in accounting, in formative and summative work.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: When designing assessment for GenAI, modules should keep integrity and GenAI control policies under continuous review, since AI content is hard to detect; policies, including acceptable use, should be clear to all staff and students, and students should be reminded of the highest ethical and professional standards.

forPractitioner.text: Review GenAI and integrity policies continuously, state acceptable use clearly to staff and students, and remind students of the profession's ethical standards.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: The standards at each level are not universal competence standards; a provider developing competence standards under the Equality Act 2010 may draw on the statement and PSRB requirements and should then follow the Equality and Human Rights Commission's latest guidance.

forPractitioner.text: Do not read the standards as competence standards; if you write competence standards, use the statement and PSRB requirements and follow current EHRC guidance.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: Most students are expected to do much better than the threshold; the standards should be read and applied with the understanding that each provider decides what evidence each class of degree needs.

forPractitioner.text: Apply the standards as a guide, not a mark scheme: your institution sets the evidence each class needs, and most students should exceed the threshold.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the people who design and run it, not a standard the student reaches

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates at the threshold level
statements.paraphrase: A basic grasp of why accounting matters critically, ethically and in context.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates have a basic grasp of accounting's critical, ethical and contextual significance.

forBeneficiary.text: For a third or a pass, at the least, you need a basic grasp of why accounting matters ethically, critically and in its wider setting.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates at the threshold level
statements.about: bringing theory into discussion of public and organisational issues
statements.paraphrase: Some capacity to bring theory, concepts and debate into discussion of public and organisational questions from several social, economic, accountability and sustainability angles.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates show some capacity to draw theory and debate into discussion of public and organisational questions from several perspectives.

forBeneficiary.text: For a third or a pass, at the least, you need some ability to bring theories and debates into a discussion of public or organisational questions, looking at them from more than one angle.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates at the typical level
statements.paraphrase: A solid grasp of accounting's critical, ethical and contextual significance.

forPractitioner.text: At the typical level, graduates have a solid grasp of accounting's critical, ethical and contextual significance.

forBeneficiary.text: For a lower second (2:2), at the least, you need a solid grasp of why accounting matters ethically, critically and in its wider setting.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates at the typical level
statements.about: bringing theory into critical discussion of public and organisational issues
statements.paraphrase: A good capacity to bring theory, concepts and debate into critical discussion of public and organisational questions from several perspectives.

forPractitioner.text: At the typical level, graduates bring theory and debate well into critical discussion of public and organisational questions from several perspectives.

forBeneficiary.text: For a lower second (2:2), at the least, you need to bring theories and debates well into a critical discussion of public or organisational questions from several angles.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates at the very-good level
statements.paraphrase: A very good grasp of accounting's critical, ethical and contextual significance.

forPractitioner.text: At the very good level, graduates have a very good grasp of accounting's critical, ethical and contextual significance.

forBeneficiary.text: For an upper second (2:1), at the least, you need a very good grasp of why accounting matters ethically, critically and in its wider setting.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates at the very-good level
statements.about: bringing theory into critical discussion of public and organisational issues
statements.paraphrase: A very good capacity to bring theory and debate into critical discussion of public and organisational questions across a wide range of perspectives, joined up and synthesised.

forPractitioner.text: At the very good level, graduates integrate theory and debate into critical discussion across a wide range of perspectives, in a joined-up, synthesised way.
